Yeah, retention-first is the right call and I think you can sell Devon on it without growth feeling buried. The reframe for Devon isn't "growth is on slide 6" — it's "growth isn't the headline anymore, durable efficient growth is." Devon wants the deck to read momentum-forward; you give him that by defining momentum as compounding durability, not raw speed. That's a stronger Series B claim anyway, because it predicts what's next instead of just describing what's past.

A few thoughts on the specific worries:

- **Retention slide.** Don't lead with logo retention — lead with NRR / cohort revenue shape and call out the post-90-day expansion behavior by name. That's the part that's hardest to fake and every Series B partner in dev tools will probe it. If you have a cohort chart that shows the ugly first quarter and then a clean ramp from month 4 onward, the picture does most of the work for you.

- **The "growth is buried" framing for Devon.** The argument in one sentence: *we proved retention → so efficient CAC payback means we can now spend into a wedge that's about to get bigger.* That sequence only makes sense in this order. If growth goes first, every number on the growth slide is contestable with no foundation under it. So the ordering isn't a stylistic preference, it's the load-bearing structure of the story. Devon will feel that.

- **Unit econ, the services-in-GM thing.** Be the one to surface it. Either split it on the slide ("software GM X%, services Y%, mix trending toward software at Z% rate") or pre-empt it in the speaker notes. Series B partners for dev tools *will* ask, and looking like you tried to slide past it costs more than just stating it. Same goes for CAC payback — it's not sexy but it's the right number, and "fine but not sexy" is a feature when your growth story is efficiency-of-growth rather than speed-of-growth.

- **If Devon really wants a growth beat early.** You could put a single topline growth number on slide 2 (no chart, just a punchy line) and save the full efficient-growth slide for after retention. That gives Devon his growth headline without it having to carry the deck. Then slide 6 isn't "growth, finally" — it's "here's how the growth story compounds once we expand the wedge."

The defense that actually holds, in case it helps: a Series B is a bet on the *shape* of the business two years from now, and "getting sturdier" is a much better predictor of that shape than "growing fast right now." Every partner has seen fast.

If it would help, I can sketch what 6 slide titles + one-line theses look like under this ordering so you have something concrete to bring to Devon. Up to you.

The frame as I hear it:

A great candidate in Q3 beats a great candidate in Q1 if Q1 means a worse round story. Worth weighing against the actual evidence you have on these specific people, not the abstract market.

**Time:** I'd suggest 7:00–8:30 PM PT (90 min, fits after a normal dinner). Holler if you'd rather 6:30 or push it later.

**What I'd bring into the review — the "backed into the story" tells in v2:**

These are the chart patterns most likely to read as reverse-engineered, given the spine and what I remember from v0/v1:

- **Retention curve.** Risk: smoothed line hides early churn; y-axis truncated to 70–100% so small drops look bigger. Ask: does it show raw cohort points, not a fit line? Y-axis starts at 0 or a clearly labeled range?
- **Net-new ARR bar.** Risk: cherry-picked window (last 4 quarters, hiding the flat Q1–Q2 stretch). Ask: full time series, quarters labeled honestly, no fancy trend overlay?
- **CAC payback.** Risk: showing only the cohorts that hit payback, hiding the 18-month ones. Ask: every cohort on the chart, or at least a range with the worst case visible?
- **Software vs. services gross margin.** Risk: stacked bar where services looks like a thin slice on top of a fat software block — services drag disappears visually. Ask: two separate bars side-by-side with the gap labeled, or at minimum services called out as its own row?
- **Cohort expansion (customers expanding after day 90).** Risk: only the expanders shown, base invisible. Ask: shown as a % of the cohort with absolute N, not a logo montage?
- **Any TAM/market slide if it's still in.** Risk: nested TAM/SAM/SOM circles. That one alone signals "we backed into this."

- Core cohort usage: better than topline, with the specific reason (whatever the actual filter is)

- Path to closing: instrumentation work, Looker/CSV reconciliation, with rough timing

INCIDENT — 2023-03-15, end-of-day deploy
Written 21:00 PT, mid-response. Status: rolled back via edge flag, stragglers draining from worker queue.

What shipped
- Ten-line change on the EOD release schedule. Diff looked routine.

Repro
1. Request lands on the new path.
2. Cache miss.
3. Falls through to the old entitlement check.
4. Retries against the worker pool.
5. Piles up there.

Why it broke
- Asymmetric blast radius. Only some tenants hit the bad branch. When they do, one inbound request fans out into ~6–8 internal calls.
- Diff size did not match the failure surface. "Tiny diff" was actively misleading here.

Why we didn't see it sooner
- Dashboards looked half-normal for too long. Aggregate metrics masked the tenants running on the bad branch. By the time it was obvious, the queue was already deep.

Response so far
- Devon: on traces.
- Priya: rolled traffic back from the edge flag.
- Stragglers: jobs already in the worker queue continue to reprocess until the queue drains. Flag is back; queue depth is the only thing still moving.

Retro commitments
- No branchy auth/entitlement changes shipped behind a flag without a replay against prod-like traffic first. The flag was the safety net and it didn't catch this because we never exercised the bad branch under load.
- Late EOD pushes are not a casual slot. This one was small by line count, large by fan-out, and almost got treated as routine. That's the proximate cause.

Holding the bar at "demonstrated boring-and-fast, not theoretical" is the right call — the retro already named the actual pain (handoffs, checklists, human toggles), and the 4:40 bravery is just what those gaps produce at the end of a long week. Theoretical rollback paths are exactly the kind of thing that look fine in a doc and then aren't when someone's tired and the diff is small and the flag is "just this one thing."

A few things worth thinking through before you commit to next week's cutoff:

- **What "boring" actually has to look like.** If the answer is "one button, one person, tested rollback in staging against a real flag flip," that's a concrete bar. If it's "we have a runbook," that's still theoretical. Worth deciding which one before someone argues they've already met it.

- **The 4:40 problem is structural.** Late-week deploys aren't brave because people are reckless — they're brave because that's the only window between "thing is ready" and "let's not do this on Friday." A real cutoff probably needs an earlier-in-the-week default, not just a Friday ban. Otherwise you just push the bravery to Thursday 4:40.

- **One-path-to-prod was the retro's other point.** If the rollback is clean but the path to prod still has three human handoffs and a Slack ping, you fixed half the problem. Worth checking these aren't being decoupled.

- **Not making it policy today is correct.** Anything you write down Friday afternoon on a process change is going to read differently Monday. A week of "does this actually feel boring and fast when we use it" beats a written policy that calcifies around whatever was true on March 23.

Clerk
- what it is: hosted auth-as-a-service with prebuilt UI components
- upsides: ships fastest, MFA/social/SSO/email included, clean DX
- biggest worry: MAU-priced lock-in, painful to migrate later

Auth0
- what it is: mature identity platform (Okta), broad protocol support
- upsides: enterprise SSO/SAML/SCIM out of box, battle-tested, deep integrations
- biggest worry: pricing gets punitive past mid-scale, config surface is heavy

Custom
- what it is: in-house session/token logic, users stored in our own DB
- upsides: full control, no per-MAU fees, fits our schema exactly
- biggest worry: easy to underbuild security, blast radius is all ours

DECISION-PREP READ — Mercury pricing models (pure MAU / pure seat / hybrid floor + bands)

TRADEOFF YOU'RE SETTLING
  - Pure MAU: honest about the live ramp; gives Devon almost nothing to forecast against in month 1, and procurement will push back on a number that looks thin against the directory.
  - Pure seat/directory: clean PO framing; charges the org chart, not the rollout. Overstates value in every one of these accounts because all three design partners run with a directory that is materially larger than real active usage.
  - Hybrid (platform floor + active-developer bands): the only sketch that gives Devon a floor he can take to procurement AND tracks actual ramp; not free — needs a counting rule for "active developer" and a band structure, not a point estimate.

SIDE-BY-SIDE ON THE ACTUAL ACCOUNTS (numbers from Devon's export)
  Evergreen Bank
    - Live now: 14 invited users. Directory: materially larger, not quantified.
    - Pure MAU charges: 14.
    - Pure seat charges: directory size (unknown, certainly much higher than 14).
    - Hybrid next-likely band: 45-60. Expansion case: 110-130.
    - This is the row where pure-seat most obviously overstates value.
  Design partner A
    - M1: 9-14 active. M3 expected: 35-55.
    - Pure MAU M1 = 9-14, M3 = 35-55.
    - Pure seat = broader org access (overstates M1, matches later if rollout lands).
    - Hybrid follows the ramp honestly with a floor underneath.
  Design partner B
    - M1: 18-24 active. M3 expected: 60-90.
    - Directory materially larger than real active usage.
    - Same shape as A at slightly higher volume — seat-based pricing would overstate month-1 reality here too.

WHAT EACH MODEL ACTUALLY MISSES (concretely, not abstractly)
  - Pure MAU: low month-1 number looks lightweight to enterprise procurement; revenue swings as ramps land or stall; no anchor for forecasting.
  - Pure seat: prices theoretical access; undercharges expansions where a small live group drives a lot of value (the Mercury thesis); risks needing odd usage caps later because the seat isn't doing the work.
  - Hybrid: counting-rule risk — if "active developer" drifts toward directory seat, it becomes pure-seat with extra steps. Band structure has to be settled, not guessed per deal.

WHAT TO BRING TO DEVON ON TUESDAY
  - The floor question (the only one that actually settles the model):
      What number does finance actually need to forecast against for month-1 procurement conversations? Once we name that, the floor is set and the bands hang under it.
      Suggested shape: model MAU/ramp as bands (e.g. low/mid/high), not a point estimate. Same pattern Morgan used for the auth provider MAU modeling — point estimates are hand-waves.
  - The counting-rule question:
      What counts as "active developer"? Must not be directory seat. Simplest honest version: someone who has either connected a real source or completed a first live sync within the window (matches the corrected May 24 Mercury activation definition — sample imports don't count).
      Worth surfacing that the May 24 activation rule already exists for reporting; reusing it as the pricing counting rule means dashboards and billing agree by construction.
  - The band structure:
      How many bands, how wide, and how do we handle the jump from month-1 to month-3 (e.g. the Evergreen 14 → 45-60 step)? Bands need to be wide enough that mid-ramp customers don't ping us about crossing thresholds every week.

WHAT'S MISSING / CAN'T BE ANSWERED YET
  - Evergreen's full directory size is described as "much larger" but not quantified. Without it, the pure-seat number for Evergreen can't even be modeled concretely. Worth asking Devon if he can pull the actual directory count, or whether procurement has the number on their side.
  - Partner A and Partner B are anonymized; we don't know the directory sizes for them either. Same gap.
  - We don't have month-6 or month-12 data for any of these. The bands are month-1 to month-3 only; long-tail retention shape still belongs in a separate conversation, not this one.
  - Finance's actual forecasting requirement (the floor number) hasn't been stated yet — that's the input Devon needs to bring or that you two need to settle Tuesday before the model locks.

DECISION SURFACE FOR TUESDAY (not the answer — the questions)
  - What is the floor number finance needs? Once named, the rest of the model is mechanical.
  - What counts as an active developer for billing? Reuse the May 24 activation rule unless Devon has a reason to diverge.
  - Bands or point estimate? Bands, given how much the month-1 to month-3 step varies across these three accounts.
  - Where does the seat-count line sit in the customer conversation — do we expose it as "directory context" only, not as the priced unit? Probably yes; keeps the conversation honest and protects against the pure-seat trap.

NOT FOR THIS MEETING
  - Investor framing. Mercury pricing is internal launch-readiness work; the round remains deferred.
  - SSO / enterprise-readiness expansion. Scope for a later wave.
  - Long-tail retention shape. Bands get us through month-3; the rest is a separate problem once we have it.

Stable wrapper: three models, one tradeoff, one floor number to settle, one counting rule to reuse, bands not points. That's the smallest set of decisions that actually closes the model.

**Diagnosis (confirmed):** Morgan's read is right. The retry path uses stale cached auth context (`cached_session_version=26`, `cached_refresh_jti=rt_4b21`) while Clerk has already rotated underneath to v27/rt_4b22. The `/auth/refresh` retry then hits `session_version_mismatch` and aborts 401. The new cookie only writes *after* the failed retry, on response finalize — which is why hard reload passes.

- Hardening means existing things work more reliably, fail more honestly, and need less hand-holding. It's not "fewer features." It's a stricter bar on what ships.

Cohorts in view

- October: 27 accounts in the bounded Mercury flow. 19/27 activated within 7 days (70%). 16/27 reached first live sync within 7 days (59%).

Activation definition (plain English)
- An account counts as activated only if, within 7 days of workspace creation, one of the following happened:
  - A real data source was connected, OR
  - A first live sync completed.
- "Reached first live sync" requires the sync to have actually completed within 7 days — not queued, not retried in progress, not preview.
- A real source connected in week one is enough to count as activated; first live sync is a separate, stricter milestone.
- What does NOT count as activation:
  - Sample-import or preview-only activity.
  - Inviting a teammate or sending an invitation (supporting activity only, not activation).
  - Selecting a source without connecting it.
  - "Source-selected-only" or any other first-week state short of a real connection or completed sync.

Read
- More accounts are clearing the real-source step in week one.
- Most accounts that clear real source are also clearing first live sync in the same window — the gap between activation and first-live-sync is small in both cohorts.
- October over September reflects cleaner first-admin setup, not a relabeling of preview activity.

Caveat (must stay on the slide)
- Expansion after initial admin/setup is still uneven.
- This slide does not imply downstream usage, retention, or revenue expansion is solved.
- Late-October cohorts do not yet support a longer-window expansion read — the framing stays week-one only.

- The gap is real-source activity, not preview, not invite-only, not source-selected-only — those states do not enter the activation count at all.

Answering your five questions off the existing September/October Mercury cohort package. No new weekly cut, no new chart.

1) Cohort construction / scope
The September and October 2023 external cohorts are bounded to accounts that entered the Mercury flow — i.e., created a workspace and proceeded into the unassisted workspace-to-first-sync path Mercury is built around. The package stays at that scope on purpose. A broader pipeline view (top-of-funnel signups, accounts that never reached the Mercury surface, invite-only accounts that did not create a workspace) is not part of this cut and is not rolled up into the cohort numbers.

2) Activation definition (outside-reader, plain language)
An account counts as activated within 7 days of workspace creation when a real source is connected within that window OR first live sync is completed within that window. The same 7-day window is used for both events, and either event on its own is sufficient.

What stays out of the activation count: sample import / preview-only behavior, invite sent, invite accepted, preview viewed, and source selected in-product without a real source completing connection. None of these count as activation, and preview/sample activity is kept separate throughout the package rather than being netted against it.

3) October: 19/27 activated within 7 days vs. 16/27 first live sync within 7 days
Confirmed. The full three-account gap is accounts that connected a real source within 7 days but did not complete first live sync within that same window. There is no other first-week transitional state folded into the gap, and the two rates are not two ways of measuring the same thing — they share the 7-day window but count different events. The same three-account pattern shows up in September (15 activated vs. 12 first live sync), so the gap is structural: real source connection routinely happens before queued/retry paths complete, not a definitional artifact.

4) Expansion / longer-window caveat
The package stays week-one focused because the late-October cohort has not matured far enough past workspace creation for a longer-window expansion read to be clean — there isn't enough post-window behavior yet for a number that isn't dominated by very recent activity. That is a cohort-maturity point, not a definitional one. Most likely path: the replay harness is exercising only the Clerk-payload → webhook-normalize leg and is NOT running the post-normalize enrichment that pulls workspace from Scaffold's own DB (likely a `workspace_members` / external_id mapping). Live create yesterday worked because the live path runs that lookup; replay doesn't, because it's replaying Clerk bytes only with no Scaffold-side enrichment. So `workspace_claim` is genuinely absent from what the replay pipeline ever sees — not because Clerk failed to send it, and not because the JWT builder dropped it, but because the replay scope is narrower than the live path.

Why it's probably not the two framings you named:

- Clerk payload issue, in the strong sense, is unlikely. The `metadata_keys=[email,role,last_login]` line is the giveaway — that's our normalizer's extraction list, not Clerk's payload shape. If workspace lived under `public_metadata` / `private_metadata` / `unsafe_metadata` / `organization` and our normalizer were configured to read it, you'd see it here (or a null), not `<missing>` with workspace absent from the keys entirely. A real Clerk-payload issue would look like: workspace field present in raw body, value empty/wrong, normalizer faithfully reading empty.
- JWT mapping bug, in the strict "builder doesn't read what the normalizer wrote" sense, is also unlikely. The normalizer never wrote `workspace_claim` to begin with — it's `<missing>` upstream of `jwt.build`, so there's nothing for the builder to misread. `JWT_METADATA_MISMATCH` here is downstream of a real upstream absence, not a wiring bug.

So the real fault sits between your two framings: replay-scope divergence. The replay test, as currently built, isn't replaying the full live sequence.

Discriminating evidence, in priority order:

1. Dump the raw Clerk webhook body for `user_7Q9` (Clerk dashboard or webhook log) for the same event the replay sourced from. If workspace/org info is present anywhere in the body (top-level, `public_metadata`, `organization`, `unsafe_metadata`), the payload carried it and our normalizer didn't pull it. If it's absent there too, Clerk didn't carry it — meaning workspace is Scaffold-side and must be joined in. Either way you've localized whether the source of truth is Clerk or our DB.
2. Compare normalized output of yesterday's passing live create against today's replay normalize. If the live one shows extra fields/keys the replay one doesn't, the divergence is in what each path runs after the byte-for-byte Clerk payload — confirms enrichment-skip on replay.
3. Grep the webhook handler for source/replay branching. Likely shape: `if event.source != "replay": workspace_lookup.run(...)` or a flag gating the workspace join. If you find it, that's the bug and the fix is one branch.
4. Direct probe: replay the same event but force the post-normalize workspace lookup to run. If `workspace_claim` populates and `jwt.build` succeeds, the missing step is confirmed and the assertion was measuring the wrong boundary.

What this implies for the harness:

Replay currently tests Clerk-bytes → webhook normalize. It does not test the full live sequence. If workspace is determined by Scaffold-side state, then "replay can never produce a workspace claim" unless either (a) the harness includes the DB enrichment step, or (b) the test seeds the workspace mapping and replays only the bytes that should carry workspace through the path. As written, the assertion is failing because it's measuring a path that was never going to carry that field — a test-scope problem, not (yet) a code-path bug.

Narrow next move: run check 1 first — free and tells you whether the source of truth is Clerk-side or Scaffold-side. If Scaffold-side, the fix is in the replay harness (include the enrichment or seed the mapping), not in the webhook handler or JWT builder. Don't patch the normalizer or JWT mapping to compensate; that papers over a test-scope gap with a code change that drifts the live path. This is the same shape as the Mar 15 lesson — replay-vs-prod divergence, flag-only branchy path, unexercised step not being a safety net.

Subject: Re: Pinecone connector verification docs wording

Hi,

Thanks for the follow-ups. Answers below, scoped to the current API v2 quickstart and our supported connector/auth model. Nothing here changes the connector header contract we already confirmed (`X-Scaffold-Workspace` + `X-Scaffold-Signature`, header-only, no query-param fallback).

1) Cursor stability across retries
   Per the API v2 quickstart, pagination cursors are intended to be replayable: the same `after` cursor on the same connection should return the same page (or advance deterministically) as long as the underlying dataset hasn't changed. For a transient auth failure on a previously successful page, retrying the same `after` cursor is the supported path. If you get an auth error mid-page and the page never completed, restart from the prior successful page's `endCursor` rather than re-issuing the original first-cursor query — that keeps the boundary between "page N+1 retry" and "rewind to page 1" clean.

2) JWT expiry during a connector retry
   Refresh credentials first, then replay the same GraphQL operation as a new request (same variables, same operation name). The API v2 contract treats a replayed operation with a fresh credential as a new authenticated request, not a continuation of the expired one — there's no server-side resume token. Don't try to attach the new token to a half-completed prior request; just re-send.

3) In-place rotation of workspace-scoped tokens
   Today's supported path is to issue a new workspace-scoped token via the same workspace token endpoint you've already used and replace the active token on your side; the customer does not need to go through a full reconnect for the connector to keep working, since the connector verifies against `X-Scaffold-Signature` over the request body. We don't have a separate in-place rotation endpoint today, and we aren't committing to one as part of this conversation. If a workspace is being decommissioned (e.g., ownership transfer), that's a different path and worth a separate thread.

Draft for the Pinecone quickstart retry/JWT section (additions only, scoped to the already-accepted paragraph):

---

Retry and JWT examples

The following short examples extend the supported retry behavior for the API v2 GraphQL/JWT connector path. None of them add a new endpoint, header, or auth surface; they describe how clients use the existing path.

1) Paginated GraphQL request after JWT expiry

If a paginated GraphQL request returns 401 because the JWT has expired, the client refreshes the JWT and replays the same page with the same cursor. Pagination does not restart from the prior successful page.

    // Same cursor, same page; only the JWT is fresh.
    page, _ := client.GraphQL.Query(ctx, listDocs, cursor, newJWT)
    for page.Next {
        cursor = page.EndCursor
        page, _ = client.GraphQL.Query(ctx, listDocs, cursor, newJWT)
    }

2) Mutation that fails auth before resolver execution

If a mutation returns 401 before the resolver runs, treat the failed request as having no side effect. Refresh the JWT and replay the same mutation with the same variables; the retry is clean.

    // 401 before resolver == no side effect. Replay once with a fresh JWT.
    err := client.GraphQL.Mutate(ctx, createDoc, vars, newJWT)
    if isAuthPreResolver(err) {
        err = client.GraphQL.Mutate(ctx, createDoc, vars, newJWT)
    }

3) Unsupported token-rotation headers

Token-rotation headers are not part of the current connector path and are not honored if present.

---

WEBHOOK SIGNING — VERIFYING DELIVERIES, ROLLING SECRETS, HANDLING TEST EVENTS

How Atlas signs a delivery

Every webhook delivery carries:

  - Atlas-Timestamp: the Unix-second time at dispatch
  - Atlas-Signature: HMAC-SHA256(your_endpoint_secret, "<timestamp>.<raw_body>")
  - Atlas-Event-Id: a stable identifier for that delivery

The signed string is the timestamp, a single "." separator, and the raw request body bytes, concatenated in that order. The "raw body" is the byte sequence Atlas sent — not a parsed-and-re-serialized version of it. Parsing the JSON and re-stringifying it (even with the same library) changes whitespace, key order, or escaping and produces a different byte sequence, which is the most common cause of signature mismatches reported to support. Sign and verify against the bytes you actually received.

Verification steps

  1. Capture the raw request body bytes before any JSON parser, middleware, or framework sees it.
  2. Read the Atlas-Timestamp header as an integer.
  3. Read the Atlas-Signature header.
  4. Reject if the timestamp is outside your endpoint's tolerance window. Tolerance is for clock-skew accommodation; see the section below for the rationale.
  5. Compute HMAC-SHA256(your_endpoint_secret, "<timestamp>.<raw_body>") and compare against the header value using a constant-time comparison.
  6. Accept only if the comparison matches and the timestamp is inside tolerance.

Reference pseudocode:

        raw = read_request_body_bytes()         # before parsing
        ts  = int(headers["Atlas-Timestamp"])
        sig = headers["Atlas-Signature"]

        if abs(now() - ts) > TOLERANCE:         # see your endpoint config
            reject("timestamp outside tolerance")

        expected = hmac_sha256(secret, f"{ts}.{raw}".encode())
        if not constant_time_eq(expected, sig):
            reject("signature mismatch")

        accept(raw)

Timestamp tolerance

The tolerance window exists to absorb normal clock drift between distributed systems. It is not a security bypass. It does not allow old or replayed events through, and it does not weaken the replay protection that signing the timestamp provides — the signed timestamp is what stops replays; tolerance only adjusts for legitimate NTP skew between your server and ours. A delivery far outside tolerance is almost always a clock-sync problem on the receiver side, not an Atlas issue, and is not grounds to assume the signature is stale or that Atlas is sending an old payload.

If you are consistently failing tolerance, check your server's clock against a known-good NTP source before opening a ticket.

Rotating webhook secrets

Atlas supports a two-slot secret: a current secret and, during a rotation window, a previous secret. During the rotation window, deliveries verify against either slot. Once the window closes, Atlas stops emitting the previous-secret signature and you should drop that slot from your verification path.

Verification during rotation:

  1. Compute the expected signature against the current secret.
  2. If it does not match, compute against the previous secret.
  3. Accept if either matches. Reject only if both fail.

This avoids the most common rotation failure: a fleet of customer workers picking up the new secret at different times. If your verification path only knows the new secret, deliveries handled by workers that haven't yet rolled will fail intermittently during the window. Verifying against both slots for the duration of the window is the supported pattern.

Test-mode events

Test-mode events are signed with the same secret, the same headers, and the same algorithm as live events. There is no separate test secret and no alternate signing path. They are distinguishable by payload:

  - The body contains `"livemode": false`.
  - The Atlas-Event-Id carries a recognizable test prefix.

Integration guidance:

  - Verify the signature exactly as for a live event — signing does not change in test mode.
  - Then inspect `livemode` in the parsed body before deciding what to do with the event.
  - Route test events to a separate sink, environment, or dry-run handler during integration. Do not let test events drive production side effects, because customers commonly replay historical test events during bring-up, and an unguarded handler will take real action on them.

If verification still fails

Before escalating, support should collect:

  - A copy of the raw request as Atlas sent it: method, full path, all Atlas-* headers, and the raw body bytes (or a SHA-256 of the body if it is large). A single HTTP server log line with all of the above is the most useful artifact you can ask for.
  - The customer's verification code (or pseudocode), the language, and the HMAC library in use.
  - The secret ID currently configured on the endpoint, and whether a rotation happened recently.
  - The customer's clock source and the observed time delta between their server and the Atlas-Timestamp header on a failing delivery.

If those don't resolve it, route to Atlas's first technical read with the artifacts above. Do not speculate about the cause beforehand — the most common root cause is on the receiver side (a body-rewriting middleware, an NTP drift, or a worker that hasn't picked up a rotated secret), and unsupported speculation tends to send customers down the wrong path.

Why "non-binding roadmap appendix" still isn't safe

  - "Non-binding" gets read by procurement, security review, and future Scaffold folks as a polite fiction once it's in the renewal paper trail.
  - "Roadmap appendix" creates a discoverable, attributable artifact that gets cited next renewal cycle, in QBRs, and in any later escalation about whether we "said" this was coming.
  - Even a soft, disclaimed appendix becomes the answer when someone asks "did we promise Evergreen granular sync-operator?" — yes, it's in the schedule we signed.
  - It still functions as a renewal-adjacent commitment. The disclaimed tone doesn't undo the attribution.

Patterns to delete entirely from the appendix

  - "non-binding roadmap appendix," "forward-looking appendix," "informational appendix"
  - "anticipated," "planned," "under consideration," "expected to evaluate," "may be explored"
  - "subject to future development," "to be determined," "to be assessed during the term"
  - any clause tying granular sync-operator to the annual term, renewal cycle, or "during the contract period"
  - "Customer has expressed interest in..." — acknowledges the ask inside the contract itself
  - "Vendor acknowledges Customer's request for..." — same problem
  - "Scaffold will continue to evaluate..." — directional commitment even without a date
  - any timeline hint ("Q2 2026," "later in the term," "during the renewal year")
  - any reference to the January 6 review meeting by name — turns the meeting into a commitment surface

  - Plain descriptive title: "Current Mercury Administrative Controls" or "Current Admin Surface (as of renewal date)."
  - Content limited to what is shipped and supported today: SAML login, admin-audit history lookup, invite / source / admin UI controls, standard support paths.
  - No references to granular sync-operator, advanced admin, role editor, permission customization, or "Customer-requested capabilities."
  - No future tense about admin scope.
  - One closing line worth keeping: "Capabilities not described in this appendix or the order form are not part of the current term." That's the negative space that prevents the granular request from being implied by omission.

---

**Common JWT verification failures**

If Atlas is rejecting a token you generated, work through the checks below in order. These are the differences we see most often in support cases, and they are configuration differences on your side rather than a change in how Atlas accepts tokens.

- **Clock skew on `iat`, `nbf`, or `exp`.** If your server's clock is even a few minutes ahead of Atlas's, a token can be rejected because `iat` or `nbf` is in the future or `exp` is already in the past. Use NTP on the host that signs tokens, and confirm the time Atlas sees matches what you used to set the claims.
- **Stale signing key after rotation, or `kid` mismatch.** If you rotated your signing key, make sure the verifier Atlas uses points at the new key (or the JWKS endpoint that publishes it) and that the token's `kid` resolves. A cached old key is the usual cause right after a rotation.
- **Signing secret or algorithm mismatch.** Confirm the secret or private key you sign with is the one Atlas expects for this workspace and environment, and that the algorithm in your header (`alg`) matches what Atlas is configured to verify. Mismatches here look the same as a wrong secret.

If those checks don't resolve it, include the unredacted token (or a sample with the same shape and claims), the workspace and environment, the rough timestamp, and the verifier configuration in your support ticket and Atlas support will take a look.

Publishable paragraph

If a request signed with a JSON Web Token fails verification in Atlas, the place to look is the calling system's configuration rather than Atlas. Common causes include clock skew between the signing host and Atlas, which can put `iat`, `nbf`, or `exp` outside the accepted window; a signing key that no longer matches what Atlas expects after rotation, including a `kid` mismatch; and a signing secret or algorithm that has drifted from what is configured for the workspace. Walking through these checks typically identifies the cause, and adjusting the calling system resolves the issue without any change on the Atlas side.

Claims to avoid

  - Any wording that says Atlas "changed," "updated," "tightened," "now requires," or "behaves differently" around JWT verification, including date anchors like "in January" or "recently."  
  - Framing the paragraph as a response to a Scaffold-side incident or fix ("we fixed," "we identified an issue," "post-incident guidance").  
  - Ranking the checks ("the most common cause is…", "this usually means a wrong signing secret"). List them flat.  
  - Overstated language: "fixed," "prevents," "guaranteed," "enterprise-ready," "robust," "hardened."  
  - Promising Atlas behavior it does not have ("we'll retry," "we'll accept older tokens," "we allow a skew window").  
  - Mentioning Compass, internal owner-action context, or any internal-only tooling; this is customer docs.  
  - Implying the customer is "doing it wrong" in a way that contradicts the "config diff on your side, not a change in how Atlas accepts tokens" framing; keep it neutral.

That draft misses the constraints set when the JWT support macro was corrected on Jan 30. Specific issues:

1. "Most JWT verification errors mean the signing secret... is wrong" — ranks signing secret first. Required: flat, non-ranked list. Recent tickets were 2 clock-skew (iat/nbf), 1 stale-key post-rotation, 0 Atlas incidents — "most" is not defensible.

2. "Scaffold JWT semantics were updated in January 2026 to reject stale tokens more aggressively" — implies a platform change, a recent auth change, and new behavior. Must be removed. The customer-facing line must say these are config differences on their side "rather than a change in how Atlas accepts tokens."

3. Missing required causes: clock skew on iat/nbf/exp, and stale signing key after rotation including kid mismatch. Both must appear in the list.

4. "Configured in Scaffold" framing — the signing secret lives on the customer's side. "Signing-secret mismatch between what your app uses and what Atlas has on file" is the correct shape.

5. None of the banned words (fixed / prevents / guaranteed / enterprise-ready) appear, so that part is fine. Keep it that way.

Corrected paragraph:

If Atlas rejects a JWT, the cause is a configuration difference on your side rather than a change in how Atlas accepts tokens. Things to check:

  - Clock skew affecting the iat, nbf, or exp claims
  - A stale signing key after rotation, including a kid mismatch
  - A signing-secret or algorithm mismatch between what your app uses to sign and what Atlas has on file

Confirm your app is signing with the current key and secret. If verification still fails after these checks, contact Scaffold support with the failing token's header and claims (without sharing the signing secret).

apply to on-call pages, the #support-rotation channel, and dashboard

DEFINITIONS
  Endpoint-local: retry traffic generated by a single workspace or

  Queue-wide: aggregate Atlas delivery metrics (p95 latency, drop

    • A single workspace crosses retry/concurrency thresholds across

    • A cluster of endpoint-local 5xx retries across unrelated
      workspaces in a short window, still no queue-wide movement.
    • Any customer-impacting soft signal that has not crossed P0.

    • Single-workspace endpoint 500s or intermittent retries.
    • One customer's setup noise (sandbox dual-subscription, mis-
      configured receiver, parsing-then-resigning, etc.).
    • Workspace-local retry-queue contention that recovers inside
      the dashboard's normal envelope.

Only on (a) sustained P0, (b) dropped events traced to Atlas, or

  • The guardrail still reduces retry-queue contention during noisy

    language in dashboards, macros, or customer replies.

             verification, JWT/webhook macro hygiene.

**Bottom line: do NOT list top five supported sources in the empty state.** Keep the help affordance as a single docs link on the brand-new-workspace path only, exactly as already locked. Salesforce sandbox and NetSuite questions go to the docs page, not the UI.

## 1. Should we list the top five sources in the empty state?

No. Decoupling rationale:

- **Scope creep.** The Feb 26 lock-in was docs discovery only. Listing top-N sources in the empty state reopens the surface and creates a new product promise — what we *say* we support at first touch.
- **Asymmetric cost.** A docs link is cheap and reversible. An embedded list forces version coordination with the source-types page, opens "you listed X but not Y" complaints, and invites roadmap pressure ("when's Salesforce sandbox?"). Every new list entry becomes a future de-list decision.
- **Brand-new vs. cancel vs. provider-context-lost are different states.** The link already lives only on the brand-new-workspace path. A source list would tempt us toward the cancel/context-lost paths too — that's exactly the merge you (correctly) want to prevent.
- **No activation evidence yet.** We have no data on whether listing sources moves a workspace to real-source-connected or first-live-sync. Embedding it before we have even a directional read is putting a thumb on the scale without a hypothesis.

## 2. Where the detail should live instead

- **In-app:** Keep the title `No connected sources yet`, body `Connect your first source to start syncing`, and a single `See supported source types` link on the brand-new-workspace path only. No link on the cancel-auth or provider-context-lost paths.
- **Docs (the canonical surface):** Maintain the supported-source-types page as the source of truth. Add — or ask docs to add — a short, factual note addressing the Salesforce sandbox and NetSuite questions that came up this week:

  - NetSuite: same standard — supported or not, with the precise connector scope. If partially supported, name what's in/out.
- **Support macro:** Add a one-liner to the support macro that points the workspace to the relevant docs section. Macro-only, no UI surface change.
- **Priya's lane:** Activation copy and onboarding UX stay in Priya. Jake owns the docs page content for supported source types and the staging parity check.

## 3. What NOT to claim in the March review

- Do not describe the empty-state work as "activating" workspaces or "driving source connections." The activation definition is unchanged: `real_source_connected OR first_live_sync_completed within 7 days`. This work is activation-*quality* UX/copy, not conversion.
- Do not describe the click-throughs on the docs link as adoption, conversion, demand signal, or a roadmap mandate. They are docs-discovery clicks.

External launch-readiness evidence (design-partner/trial feedback, repeated platform seam, independent architecture ownership) is still the gate; contained docs-discovery traffic is not it.
- Do not reclassify this work as anything other than copy/config on the existing one-screen pattern. No new permission model, no admin/granular-role work, no invite-link changes, no metric, no first-live-sync definition change.

## Why this framing is durable

The gate that held through Q1 was: narrow, reversible work; explicit owner lanes; durable records; visible caveats; no accidental commitments. Listing sources in the empty state would violate the first and last of those.   Subject: Re: API v2 JWT — "token not yet valid" right after deploy

  Hi <name>,

  Short answer: Scaffold's verifiers are not rejecting valid tokens in your case. What you're seeing is a configuration difference on your side — the example `nbf` from the docs got carried into your production template.

  - The docs example uses a fixed `nbf` value. When that's copied into a live template, the token's `nbf` lands in the past (or near-now) relative to Scaffold's server time, depending on the moment of deploy and any host clock drift.

  - Set `nbf` from your issuing host's current time, not from the docs example.

Below is a practical redline response you can hand to internal legal. Cover framing first, then the proposed replacement language with optional rationale legal can strip before sending.

COVER FRAMING
  - Preserves what the customer actually needs: predictable support, real defect fixes, advance notice of connector changes.
  - Replaces the open-ended warranty with our standard "material conformance to documentation" warranty scoped to connectors we make generally available.
  - Removes the per-event service-credit obligation and routes any credits to the existing SLA exhibit (whatever Exhibit X says — usually uptime, capped at a small percentage of monthly fees).
  - Carves out, explicitly, the four categories you named: customer-side permissions, source-system changes, unsupported connectors, setup mistakes.
  - Keeps connector evolution under our control with a 90-day notice commitment (with narrow exceptions for security, third-party breaking changes, legal/regulatory) — not a customer veto.
  - Sarah is the standing CC on external legal/procurement correspondence — add her when this goes to the customer.


PROPOSED REPLACEMENT LANGUAGE

[Customer's clause]
"Provider warrants that all listed source connectors are production-ready for Customer's use cases during the subscription term. If Customer's first-source sync fails due to Provider connector limitations, Provider will apply service credits for the affected month. Provider will maintain support for Customer's selected connectors through the subscription term and will not remove or materially change connector behavior without Customer's written approval."

[Provider's proposed replacement]
"During the subscription term, the Service will perform in material conformance with the then-current Provider documentation. Provider will use commercially reasonable efforts to make generally available source connectors operable in accordance with such documentation.

Customer acknowledges that successful source synchronization depends on factors Provider does not control, including: (i) Customer's selection of a source connector that Provider documents as supported for general availability; (ii) Customer's configuration of that connector and the granting of all required permissions, scopes, and credentials on the source system; (iii) the source system's continued availability, operation, and compatibility; and (iv) the absence of breaking changes by the third-party source provider that materially affect connector behavior. Provider has no obligation with respect to sync failures, data issues, or service unavailability caused in whole or in part by: (a) use of connectors not documented as supported for general availability; (b) customer-side permissions, scopes, credentials, or configuration; (c) setup or configuration errors by Customer or its users; (d) changes to, unavailability of, or incompatibilities with the third-party source system; or (e) any other cause outside Provider's reasonable control.

If Customer reasonably believes a sync issue is caused by a confirmed platform defect, Customer may open a support ticket through Provider's standard support channels. Provider will triage and respond according to its then-current support severity and response-time table, and will work in good faith to remediate confirmed defects through updates, patches, configuration guidance, or documented workarounds. Service credits, if any, are governed exclusively by the service-level agreement attached as Exhibit [X] (the "SLA") and are not available for events outside the SLA's scope, including source-connector setup, configuration, permissions, source-system changes, or use of unsupported connectors.

Provider may add, modify, deprecate, or retire a generally available connector from time to time. For material changes that Provider reasonably expects to disrupt Customer's active use of a connected source, Provider will provide Customer with at least ninety (90) days' prior written notice (which may be delivered by release notes, email to Customer's admin contact, or in-product notification), except where a shorter period is reasonably necessary to address a security risk, a third-party source provider's breaking change, or a legal or regulatory requirement. This Agreement does not require Provider to obtain Customer's consent for any such change."


OPTIONAL RATIONALE — legal can delete before sending

  On the warranty: A warranty that runs for the full subscription term and covers "Customer's use cases" converts every customer use case into a warranty trigger and effectively turns the connectors into a bespoke build. Replacement is the standard "material conformance to documentation" formulation, which preserves the obligation to deliver what was promised without making each customer's intended use a warranty standard.

  On service credits: Per-event credits for first-source sync failures are not how service credits function in a SaaS contract — credits attach to platform-level SLA breaches (uptime, response), are capped, and are the customer's exclusive remedy. The great majority of first-sync failures fall into one of the four categories above (permissions, source-system state, setup, unsupported connector) and are not Provider-side defects. Replacement routes credits to the existing SLA exhibit and explicitly excludes the four categories.

  On the no-change-without-consent clause: A unilateral customer veto over connector evolution would block Provider from retiring unsupported integrations, responding to third-party breaking changes, or shipping improvements, and would create a roadmap hostage situation on a small deal. Replacement preserves the customer's interest in predictability through a 90-day prior-notice commitment with narrow, objectively-defined exceptions (security, third-party breaking change, legal/regulatory) while keeping product evolution under Provider's control. The 90-day window is industry-standard for connector deprecation notices.


NOTES FOR LEGAL

  - The SLA cross-reference assumes Exhibit X exists and is the standard support/uptime exhibit. If this deal does not yet have an SLA exhibit attached, that needs to be drafted separately and referenced in this clause — flag before sending.
  - The four rejection categories (a)–(e) map 1:1 to what you specified. If customer counsel pushes back on the breadth of (e) ("any other cause outside Provider's reasonable control"), it is a standard force-majeure-style catchall and easy to defend.
  - If the deal is small enough that legal wants a softer posture on the 90-day notice, that is the easiest place to give (60 days is the typical compromise). Do not soften on the credit carve-out or on the absence of a consent right.
  - Sarah should review before the redline goes to customer counsel — she owns customer-thread wording and is the standing CC per the external communications rule.

Quick narrowing on this:

- Our signing is HMAC-SHA256 over the raw request body; your delivery logs match what we sent, so the mismatch is most likely being introduced between receipt and verification on your side.
- Most common cause: middleware that calls `JSON.parse` on the body before your verify step, then re-serializes for downstream handlers — re-serialization changes bytes (whitespace, key order, Unicode escapes) and breaks the signature.
- To confirm: dump the exact raw bytes received before any parser touches them, recompute HMAC against those bytes with your signing secret, and compare to the `X-Scaffold-Signature` header. If raw matches and parsed doesn't, the bug is in the body-parsing path.
- Audit which middleware runs before your verify step — JSON body parsers, request loggers, content negotiators, proxies that buffer or transform bodies — and confirm your verify helper receives the raw body, not a parsed object.
- If a fresh delivery's raw bytes still don't match the signature header, share the delivery ID and a redacted timestamp from your side and we'll re-check that specific delivery from our end.

Sidebox — JWT sample timestamps

The `nbf` (and `iat`) values in this tutorial's code samples are illustrative only. Atlas v2 accepts a clock-skew tolerance of approximately five minutes between the token-issuing host and Atlas for `nbf`, `iat`, and `exp`.

When adapting these samples into your own code:

- Generate `nbf` from the issuing host's current time at request time; do not paste the sample value.
- Confirm the issuing host's clock is synchronized via NTP.
- Verify `kid`, signing key, and algorithm match your registered Atlas credentials.

A "token not yet valid" error after copying a sample timestamp is typically a clock-skew or sample-timestamp issue on the issuing side, not an Atlas platform change.

Subject: Re: duplicate webhook deliveries

Hi [name],

Thanks for sending this over — worth walking through carefully.

Scaffold webhooks are at-least-once. When your endpoint doesn't return a 2xx (timeout, 5xx, dropped connection), the same delivery is retried, and the event_id is identical across retries. Consumers are expected to dedupe on event_id before processing; the most common reason duplicates surface in your logs is the handler returning a 2xx after our worker has already timed out the read, or the connection dropping before the 2xx lands.

If you'd like me to confirm on our side, send a couple of the duplicated event_ids with rough delivery timestamps and I'll check whether they're distinct deliveries of the same event (expected) versus two distinct events that happen to share a payload (which would be a real issue and I'd want to chase). The current path treats event_id as the unique delivery key, so I don't expect to find non-unique IDs in the logs, but I'll verify against the actual events.

— Leo

To: customer (cc support thread)
From: Support / Sarah
Subject: Re: /sources adjacent-response overlap during live sync

Hi [name],

Thanks for the polling detail. Before we draw any conclusion about /sources behavior, a quick note on the cursor contract and what we need from you to check the case.

The /sources endpoint returns a page of results plus a next_cursor (or null when there are no more results). Two facts about how that works during a live sync:

  - A request without a next_cursor starts a fresh read and returns the first page of that new read. It is not a continuation of any prior walk.
  - A request with a next_cursor continues the prior walk from where that cursor left off.

Source rows are not pinned during a live sync, so if your integration alternates a fresh poll (no cursor) with a paginated walk (carrying the cursor forward), you can see the same source row in adjacent responses — once as the head of the new read, and again as you resume the prior walk. From the client that looks like a duplicate. From the server, each response is internally consistent and the row is not duplicated.

To confirm which it is, we need from you:

  - The request IDs (or X-Request-Id response headers) for the two adjacent responses.
  - The next_cursor value your integration sent on the second of the two requests — i.e., whether the second request carried a cursor from the first, or started fresh.
  - The id (or other stable key) of the source row you saw in both responses, plus the response timestamps.

With those, our first technical read on Atlas/API v2 will check the server-side responses for those request IDs to confirm whether there was a server-side duplicate or a cursor contract violation, or whether the server returned two internally consistent responses and the overlap came from the client re-issuing a fresh read. If the logs show a duplicate inside a single response or a cursor violation, we open a product investigation. If they don't, this is expected behavior under the contract and we can recommend a polling pattern that avoids the overlap.

This stays in normal Atlas/API v2 support. No escalation, no workaround, and no fix is being scheduled unless the log check above shows a server-side issue.

Best,
Sarah / Support

  Hi [name],

  Thanks for the detail on the intermittent 401s — I took a careful first read of the failing requests in our logs before responding, and what I see is consistent with clock skew on the tokens rather than a change in how Atlas verifies them.

  Specifically, the JWTs in the failing requests had `iat` and `nbf` values roughly six minutes ahead of our verifier's clock at the time of the requests. That's outside the documented leeway Atlas applies to `iat`/`nbf` claims, so those tokens would be rejected even with no other change on our side. You mentioned an NTP issue in your fleet during the deploy window, which fits the timing — if the worker minting the tokens was running ahead, the `iat`/`nbf` it emitted would be ahead by the same amount.

  A few notes on what I checked against the requests:

  - `iat`, `nbf`, and `exp` — validated against the verifier's clock with the documented leeway window; failing requests sat outside that window. This is expected behavior, not new.
  - Signing key and `kid` — matched the active key registered for your workspace; no rotation gap in our logs during the window.
  - Algorithm and secret — consistent with the configuration you have on file; no algorithm mismatch on the failing tokens.

  We didn't ship any changes to Atlas JWT verification in the window you reported, and the verifier code path on our side is the same as it has been. So our current read is that these 401s are the expected outcome of the leeway check on the tokens you sent us, not a defect in how Atlas accepts tokens.

  If that doesn't match what you observed on your side, it would help to have the following for at least one request you believe involved a token that was inside the leeway window:

  - A timestamp (with timezone) for the 401, taken from your access logs.
  - The full JWT header and payload for that token, including the `iat` and `nbf` claims — a redacted copy with those fields intact is fine.
  - The verifier-side time your app observed for that same request, from the handler that made the call.
  - The exact 401 response body and `WWW-Authenticate` header, if your client logs them.

  If a token inside the documented leeway was rejected, that would change my assessment and I'd want to dig into our side further. If everything you have lines up with clock skew, the durable fix is on the issuing worker — making sure NTP is in sync before tokens are minted, or having the issuer subtract a small offset from `iat`/`nbf` to absorb verifier drift, usually clears it up.

  Happy to keep this in support and circle back if you turn up a token you believe should have been accepted.

  Best,
  Leo

Subject: Re: JWT clock skew / leeway

Thanks for the context on the deploy pipeline.

To be direct: the documented leeway is five minutes between the token issuer's clock and the Atlas verifier, and that's the boundary the JWT contract is built around. We can't widen it per customer — token freshness semantics depend on it being narrow, and a one-off extension weakens the guarantee for everyone.

In practice, your deploy model lines up fine if time sync is settled before tokens are minted:

- Confirm NTP/chrony has converged on the host issuing the token before that step runs (or mint from a service whose clock is already synced, not from a freshly-booted host).
- Add a drift check to the deploy — even a `chronyc tracking` or `ntpq -p` right before mint catches an 8-minute offset and fails the deploy early.
- If you want a hard guardrail, have the deploy refuse to mint until drift is under 60s.
- Monitor drift on the issuing host over time so this doesn't drift back in quietly after the initial sync.

If you do see a 401 on a token that's inside the documented five-minute window — i.e., one we should have accepted — please send the request ID, the verifier-side time when it failed, and a redacted token header/payload. That's the only path that opens a real look at verification behavior on our side. Anything outside the leeway, we already know what's happening and there's nothing to investigate.

Happy to walk through the deploy sequence together if that's useful.

---

  Quick framing on how Atlas webhooks work so you can build the right pattern on your side:

  - Delivery is at-least-once. Our retry path keeps events moving through transient receiver issues (5xx, timeouts), so the same event can legitimately arrive more than once.
  - Each delivery carries a unique event_id that is reused across retries of the same event. Treat event_id as your idempotency key.
  - Verify the signature against the raw request body before processing — if you're parsing and then re-serializing the JSON, verify before the parse.

  If something on your end looks like it doesn't match that contract — e.g., different event_ids arriving for what appears to be the same underlying event, a missing signature header, or timestamps that don't line up with the documented retry window — the most useful thing is to reply here with the request IDs. Including the event_ids you saw and approximate receiver-side timestamps helps us cross-reference quickly.

Three things wrong with this draft, all on the technical claim:

1. "exactly once" is the wrong guarantee. Per the contract, webhook delivery is at-least-once and retries run up to 24 hours. The line contradicts the standing rule that documentation must not promise exactly-once, and contradicts the at-least-once framing Leo already drafted for customer-facing docs.

2. A redelivered event is not a defect. Retries reuse the same event_id for consumer idempotency, so the same event with the same event_id arriving twice is a normal retry, not a "replay defect." Putting it in the defect path also violates the rule that duplicate-delivery items don't become product-priority/defect claims unless Leo finds non-unique event_ids in the logs.

3. The duplicate-handling guidance is unsafe. Receivers should be idempotent on event_id unconditionally, not only during endpoint timeouts. The current draft under-instructs the customer and shifts the dedupe burden onto Scaffold when it belongs on the receiver.

Proposed replacement:

  Webhook delivery is at-least-once. If your endpoint returns a non-2xx response or is unreachable, we retry the same event for up to 24 hours. Each retry uses the same event_id, so your handler should be idempotent on event_id and treat any redelivery of the same event_id as a normal retry. If you believe you received a logically distinct event with a duplicated or non-unique event_id, send us the delivery logs (event_id, timestamp, request id) and we will investigate.

Subject: Re: API v2 429s during batch metadata sync

Hi [Acme contact],

Quick reply on this one — the 429s during the batch metadata sync are expected, not instability. API v2 rate-limits per workspace and returns 429 when a burst exceeds the documented budget; no data is dropped, and the response headers tell you exactly when it's safe to retry.

Headers on every API v2 response:

  - X-RateLimit-Limit — requests allowed in the current window
  - X-RateLimit-Remaining — requests left in the window
  - X-RateLimit-Reset — epoch seconds when the window resets
  - X-Request-ID — unique per request; keep this if you contact support

On a 429, the header that matters is Retry-After (when present) or X-RateLimit-Reset. That's the documented reset time. Wait until at least that timestamp before retrying, and for batch metadata we'd layer exponential backoff with jitter on top of that floor rather than retrying on a fixed interval.

Practical points for the connector:

  1. The 429s you saw are consistent with parallelizing more aggressively than usual. Batch metadata doesn't need high concurrency — capping in-flight requests per workspace keeps you comfortably under the budget.
  2. Retry-After / X-RateLimit-Reset is authoritative — don't retry before it, and don't retry on a fixed interval shorter than it.
  3. 429 bodies are JSON in the same shape as other API v2 errors, so the existing error path handles them.

When to send request IDs to support:

  - You retried after the documented reset and still got 429s
  - Headers were missing or had unexpected values
  - You saw 5xx responses alongside the 429s (different signal)
  - Anything that looks like data loss or a contract violation

For those, send the X-Request-ID values, timestamps, and a redacted response excerpt and we'll trace it. For routine 429s on a tuned batch, no request IDs are needed — the headers are the explanation.

Happy to look at a specific log snippet if useful.

Hi [name],

Thanks for the details. Based on what you've shared, these failures look like configuration differences on your side rather than a change in how Atlas accepts tokens. Three checks cover the patterns we've been seeing:

Clock skew on the issuing or verifying host
- Atlas's documented leeway on `iat`, `nbf`, and `exp` is small. Your logs show a gap of about seven minutes between the issuer and the verifier, which falls outside that window.
- Sync the host clock with NTP and confirm both sides agree.

JWKS cache after a recent key rotation
- A consumer holding a cached JWKS will keep verifying against the old `kid` until the cache refreshes.
- Force a JWKS refresh across every consumer and confirm the new `kid` is being requested.

Signing secret and algorithm
- A secret or `alg` mismatch on the verifier shows up as a verification failure independent of clock and key.
- Confirm both match what's configured for the Atlas API key.

Please re-run after the NTP sync and JWKS refresh and let us know whether the failures clear.

If you're still seeing failures after those checks, send the request IDs and timestamps and we'll take a closer look.

Paw scrape plan, not an emergency but let's be tidy about it:

- Swelling that doesn't settle by morning
- Bleeding that restarts or soaks through
- Licking that escalates instead of calming down in ~30 min
- Eating or drinking change

Subject: Re: webhook retries during metadata sync test

Hi [Name],

The duplicates you saw are the expected outcome of how our retries work — not duplicate events on our side. Quick walkthrough so we're aligned on the contract:

- Delivery is at-least-once. When your endpoint times out or returns a non-2xx, we retry the same delivery.
- Every retry for the same logical event reuses the same `scaffold-delivery-id` header. That's the idempotency key.
- Retries run with backoff up to ~24 hours, until your endpoint returns a 2xx or the window closes.

Two things to check in your handler:

1. Persist `scaffold-delivery-id` before any side effects, then dedupe on it. We don't reuse that ID across events, so a short dedupe window (minutes to a few hours) is enough.
2. Only return 2xx after the event has been committed. The two timeouts look like the handler returned (or hung) before commit, which is what triggered the retries.

If you wire that up and still see what looks like the same event delivered under different `scaffold-delivery-id` values, send us the `X-Request-Id` from each response along with the `scaffold-delivery-id` from each delivery and I'll trace it on our side. Otherwise this should resolve on your end.

Happy to jump on a quick call if it's faster than going back and forth here.

— Leo

Subject: Re: cursor_expired_after_24h — using cursors and resuming after a pause

Thanks for flagging this before changing your integration — that's the right move.

Quick answer:
- During an active page sequence, keep using the returned cursor. That's what it's for: continuing the walk without rereading the whole list.
- Cursors are short-lived (about 24 hours). If your integration pauses longer than that and then tries to reuse the original cursor, the API returns `cursor_expired_after_24h` by design.
- The fix is to persist a durable checkpoint of the last object you successfully processed during the walk, and after a long pause, restart the list from that point rather than reusing the expired cursor.

We don't recommend dropping cursors and running a full fresh poll every minute as a workaround. It doesn't make the cursor valid again — it just burns rate-limit budget and re-fetches data you've already processed.

If you put the checkpoint in place and still see `cursor_expired_after_24h` during an active sequence (no long pause), send us the request IDs and the id/timestamp of the last object you processed and we'll dig in.

— Sarah

Resolution (Sarah, support reply — same wording as the customer-facing reply):
- During an active page sequence, keep using the returned cursor until the walk completes.
- Cursors are short-lived (~24h). Persist a durable checkpoint — the id and timestamp of the last object successfully processed — during the sequence.
- After a long pause, restart the list from the last durable object boundary rather than reusing the expired cursor.
- Don't recommend dropping cursors and running a full fresh poll every minute. It doesn't make the cursor valid again, it consumes rate-limit budget, and it re-fetches already-processed objects.

Hi [name],

What you're seeing (the same event delivered twice after a 502) matches our documented webhook delivery contract: webhooks are at-least-once. We checked request IDs req_wh_9014 and req_wh_9015 on our side — both deliveries carried the same event_id, so this was the expected retry, not a duplicate from a separate path. No event was lost.

If you see behavior that doesn't fit this contract — for example, retries carrying different event_ids, or a retry after a clean 2xx — send us the request_id(s) and a timestamp window and we'll dig in.

Best,
Sarah

  Subject: Re: cursor pagination + created_after overlap

  Hi [Customer],

  Thanks for the writeup and for sending the request IDs. Leo checked
  req_cur_4418, req_cur_4419, and req_cur_4420 and confirmed those pages
  came back clean — your cursor walk was working as documented before the
  worker stopped.

  Direct answer: we don't guarantee a duplicate-free result when you mix
  a cursor walk with a fresh `created_after` poll. The two reads have
  different scopes — a cursor walks the result set you started;
  `created_after` returns events with creation timestamps at or after
  the value you pass. Events that existed before the crash sit in both
  reads, so some overlap is expected. The duplicates you're seeing are
  the boundary between the two reads, not an API defect.

  What matches the contract:

  - Walk one result set end to end with the cursor. If you need to
    pause, save a durable checkpoint — the event ID of the last record
    you processed — rather than holding the cursor.
  - On resume, continue the cursor walk while it's still valid, or
    restart from the checkpoint using `created_after` and an `event_id`
    filter. Don't run both against the same window.
  - Deduplicate on your side by event ID. Event IDs are stable, so a
    `seen_ids` set is enough.
  - If a cursor returns `cursor_expired` after a long pause, that's
    expected — restart from the checkpoint, don't reuse the old cursor.

  If you still see what looks like a server-side duplicate after
  switching to the checkpoint + dedup pattern, send us the request IDs,
  cursor values, and the duplicated event IDs and we'll dig in. The
  cursor pagination example in our docs walks through the same pattern.

  Best,

Subject: Re: Atlas API v2 — JWT verification failures after deploy

Hi [name],

Thanks for the request IDs — we reviewed req_jwt_7781, req_jwt_7782, and req_jwt_7783.

What we saw: the JWTs in those requests had `iat`/`nbf` timestamps roughly 7 minutes 12 seconds ahead of our verifier's clock at the moment of verification. The tokens are otherwise well-formed — signing, `kid`, algorithm, and claim shape all check out. So the verifier isn't rejecting them for any reason other than the timestamp window.

The contract: per the Atlas/API v2 JWT verification documentation, we allow up to 5 minutes of clock-skew leeway on `nbf`, `iat`, and `exp`. Tokens whose timestamps fall outside that window are correctly treated as not-yet-valid. We can't widen the leeway to ~10 minutes — it isn't a knob we expose per-customer, and the leeway exists to absorb small drift, not to mask a clock-sync gap in your deploy process.

What this looks like on your side: the host(s) minting tokens during/after deploy have drifted ahead of the verifier. Most often this is an NTP/chrony sync gap right when a fresh node comes up — the OS clock starts from hardware and then drifts until the time service catches it. A few practical checks that usually resolve it:

  - Confirm chronyd / systemd-timesyncd / your NTP source is enabled and reachable from the deploy environment
  - Make sure time sync completes before the token-minting service starts accepting traffic — a short wait or an explicit `ntpwait`-style gate on cold boot prevents this exact pattern
  - Add a clock-drift monitor on the minting hosts so drift shows up before it causes verification failures

To set expectations: this is a clock-skew configuration difference on your side rather than a change in how Atlas accepts tokens. We haven't changed the leeway or the verifier behavior recently, and the pattern we see on the IDs you shared is consistent with that — the gap is outside the 5-minute window.

If you do see a token rejected inside the documented 5-minute window — i.e., `iat`/`nbf` within ±5 minutes of our verifier's clock and the token still fails — please send us the request ID, a redacted token header/payload, the verifier-side timestamp from your logs, and the response body. We'll dig in.

Happy to walk through any of this on a quick call if useful.

Best,
Sarah

Subject: Re: Atlas API v2 — duplicate event IDs after pause + fresh polling

Hi [Acme team],

Thanks for the request IDs and timeline — that gave us what we needed to check.

What we saw on our side:
- `req_acme_cur_5521` and `req_acme_cur_5522`: successful cursor pages returned before the pause.
- `req_acme_poll_1189`: the fresh poll after restart; returned according to the API v2 contract.
- No server error, no data loss, no missing events on our end.

Why the duplicates appeared:
When you switch from a cursor walk (which continues from `next_cursor`) to a fresh poll anchored on `created_after`, the two reads cover an overlapping time window. The cursor pages already returned events in that window; the fresh poll will re-return them because it has no memory of the prior walk. This is how the current contract behaves — the API doesn't track what an earlier cursor walk already saw.

Recommended fix on your side:
- De-duplicate by the unique `event_id` field. Each event carries a stable ID that the API returns on every read regardless of how it was retrieved. A short-lived client-side set of seen IDs collapses the overlap.

If you see anything that doesn't fit this pattern — e.g. the same `event_id` coming back with different payloads, or events that weren't in any prior cursor page or fresh poll — please send the request IDs and a short note and we'll dig in. That's the fastest way for us to confirm whether something is outside the contract.

Happy to keep this on the existing thread.

Best,
Sarah

SUBJECT: Re: Webhook event delivered twice — review of req_wh_9041/9042/9043

Hi [name],

Thanks for sending over the request IDs. Here's what we found.

What happened on your end: req_wh_9041 returned 502 from your endpoint. Our delivery layer treats anything outside 2xx as a retry signal, so req_wh_9042 and req_wh_9043 are the retry attempts for the same logical event. All three carry the same `event_id` in the payload. That ID is stable across every retry of the same event — it's the contract.

Our contract: Scaffold webhooks are delivered at-least-once. If your endpoint returns a non-2xx (including a 5xx during a deploy), the event is retried with the same payload and the same `event_id`. We don't offer exactly-once delivery. A 502 followed by a successful retry will look like a duplicate on your side — that's documented behavior, not a defect and not a lost event. There is no data-loss indicator in our logs for this sequence.

On your side: dedupe on the payload `event_id`. If you've already processed that ID, return 2xx and drop. Each attempt also carries a unique `scaffold-delivery-id` header — that's useful for tracing a specific HTTP attempt in your logs, but it changes per retry, so it's not the idempotency key.

When to send us request IDs again: if you see retries outside the documented window, different `event_id` values for what looks like the same logical event, or a successful first attempt followed by an unexpected re-delivery, send us the request IDs (`req_wh_*`), the `event_id` values you observed, and the timestamps on your side. We'll pull the delivery logs and check whether the retry contract held.

On the IDs you sent this round: req_wh_9041, req_wh_9042, and req_wh_9043 all match the documented at-least-once retry behavior. Same `event_id` across the three. No delivery defect and no data-loss signal.

Best,
